title: The term species is arbitrary and not essentially different from variety

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The term species is arbitrary and not essentially different from variety

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The term species is given arbitrarily, for convenience, to a set of closely resembling individuals and does not differ essentially from the term variety, which is given to less distinct and more fluctuating forms.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I look at the term species, as one arbitrarily given for the sake of convenience to a set of individuals closely resembling each other, and that it does not essentially differ from the term variety, which is given to less distinct and more fluctuating forms.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter II, “Variation under Nature”; section “Doubtful species”. Scope: taxonomic practice for all organisms

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch02-06: not-empirically-resolvable, resolvability 0.28

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Datasets can measure discontinuities among organisms but cannot establish that a naming convention is arbitrary in the intended philosophical sense. No empirical outcome uniquely resolves the claim as stated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: The assertion concerns how taxonomic words are defined and whether ranks possess an 'essential' distinction; observed continuity can motivate it but cannot empirically decide a stipulative classification convention.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Arbitrary' and 'essentially different' are conceptual terms.

Any observed pattern is compatible with redefining species or variety.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The wording is partly about how a term is used, and that part does not pick out a single measurement. The biological reading, that species and varieties are not different in kind, can be proxied with public distances and ranks and has the same limits as a continuum test. Competing species concepts keep any one gap from settling the essentialist contrast, which is why discriminating power stays modest.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Treat 'no essential difference' as overlap between the divergence, reproductive isolation, and phylogenetic depth of sets named as species and sets named as varieties, and treat 'arbitrary' as inter-author discordance in rank for the same populations. A unique biological gap that taxonomists recover repeatedly would count against the statement; overlapping distributions and unstable ranks would support the empirical reading.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Different species concepts predict different gaps, so several operationalizations compete.

'Essentially' and 'for convenience' are philosophical even after a biological gap is defined.

Discordance among checklists measures nomenclatural practice as much as biology.
